evaluated.name: Dual_Peak_Capex_Dual_Moat_Deficit
evaluated.expression: SUMRANK(SUMRANK(TS_RANK(RATIO(capx, ppent), 5), TS_RANK(RATIO(capx, sale), 5)), SUMRANK(NEG(IND_ADJ(RATIO(sale, emp))), NEG(IND_ADJ(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), sale)))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Peak-intensity physical expansion confirmed on both scaling bases, in firms deficient in both pricing power and operating efficiency, identifies overinvestment without intangible support at full sample coverage.
evaluated.reasoning: This is the symmetric, full-coverage consolidation of the two proven design axes — two investment legs and two intangible legs — and gen 5 showed the margin conditioner adds alpha on top of productivity (from -5.4% to -4.7% with one denominator, with t improving in the dual-moat case). Because it needs no goodwill or R&D data it should retain coverage near 0.117 and thus be the more robust candidate if its metrics approach Signal 1's.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Dual_Peak_Capex_Low_Value_Added_Per_Worker
evaluated.expression: SUMRANK(SUMRANK(TS_RANK(RATIO(capx, ppent), 5), TS_RANK(RATIO(capx, sale), 5)), NEG(IND_ADJ(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), emp))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Gross profit per employee is the sharpest single measure of a firm's intangible capital, since it combines pricing power and labor efficiency into value added per worker; peak physical expansion by firms with low value added per worker is the cleanest overinvestment state.
evaluated.reasoning: The two conditioners that worked separately — margin and revenue per employee — are both partial views of value added per worker, so measuring it directly should dominate them in a single parsimonious leg rather than requiring two ranked legs that dilute each other. This is a substantive conditioner upgrade, not a restatement, and it keeps full coverage while reducing the signal to one investment concept and one intangible concept.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: High_Value_Added_Innovator_Capex_Restraint
evaluated.expression: SUMRANK(IND_ADJ(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), emp)), SUMRANK(RATIO(xrd, sale), NEG(TS_RANK(RATIO(capx, ppent), 5))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Firms generating high value added per worker, spending heavily on research, and holding physical capital spending below their own historical norm are compounding unrecognized intangible capital and are underpriced.
evaluated.reasoning: The long side has stabilized at roughly +3% alpha with t near 3.1 and a positive slope of about 2.4, and its weakest element is the conditioner, so substituting value added per worker for raw revenue per employee should raise the gradient by separating high-price, high-efficiency firms from low-margin revenue churners. A stronger long leg matters for the final signal because every reliable result so far is short-side driven.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Capital_Deepening_Peak_Without_Pricing_Power
evaluated.hypothesis: A five-year peak in physical capital per employee means the firm has substituted machines for people; without pricing power to monetize the new capital intensity, this deepening locks in fixed costs and depresses future returns.
evaluated.reasoning: This introduces a new investment state — the capital-labor mix rather than the flow of spending — which can be at a peak even when capex intensity is not, for instance after headcount cuts, so it tests a distinguishable form of tangible-heavy commitment. Pairing it with the margin conditioner rather than productivity avoids mechanical overlap between the employment term in both legs, and both inputs are broadly reported.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Plant_Rejuvenation_Burst_Unproductive
evaluated.hypothesis: A rising undepreciated share of gross plant means the firm has just installed a burst of new capacity relative to its existing stock; when the operator is unproductive, this newly sunk capital signals a value-destroying build cycle.
evaluated.reasoning: This repairs gen-6's Fresh_Plant_Unproductive_Operator, whose slope was the archive's strongest (-6.04) but whose alpha was negligible (t=-1.55) because a static vintage level is highly persistent and largely spanned by the FF5 investment and profitability factors; taking the annual change isolates the fresh building event, which should be far less factor-spanned and therefore carry portfolio alpha. It also tests the level-versus-change question on a stock-based capacity measure, complementing the flow-based peak results.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Peak_Capex_Low_Value_Added_Per_Worker
evaluated.hypothesis: Physical capital spending at a five-year peak relative to installed plant, undertaken by firms whose value added per worker is low for their industry, is the cleanest statement of tangible overexpansion without intangible capital to support it.
evaluated.reasoning: This fills the one untested cell of the archive's design grid: the single best-alpha investment leg paired with the best-alpha conditioner, both of which have been validated separately (alpha -5.4% with productivity; alpha t=-5.49 with value added per worker under two denominators). Parsimony matters here because each additional ranked leg has cost slope strength, so a two-leg version should retain the -5.4 FMB while capturing the value-added conditioner's alpha reliability at full coverage.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Flow_And_Vintage_Build_Burst_Unproductive
evaluated.expression: SUMRANK(SUMRANK(TS_RANK(RATIO(capx, ppent), 5), DELTA(RATIO(ppent, ppegt), 1)), NEG(IND_ADJ(RATIO(sale, emp))))
evaluated.hypothesis: A firm is unambiguously in a build cycle when its spending flow is at a multi-year peak and its plant is simultaneously getting younger relative to gross cost; unproductive operators in this state have just sunk capital they cannot monetize.
evaluated.reasoning: The vintage-change leg is an independently validated build measure (FMB -4.76, alpha -3.5%, t=-3.42) built from balance-sheet stocks rather than the cash-flow statement, so it carries information the capex flow misses — for instance disposals of old plant alongside new construction. Fusing a flow measure with a stock measure of the same economic event should sharpen the short leg more than stacking two flow normalizations did in gen 6.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Goodwill_Overhang_Low_Value_Added
evaluated.hypothesis: Acquired goodwill is impaired when the combined firm cannot generate value added per employee; goodwill-heavy firms with low gross profit per worker have demonstrably failed to realize the synergies they paid for.
evaluated.reasoning: The goodwill family holds the archive's largest alphas, and its slope responded only to productivity conditioning (from 0.05 to -2.4, then -2.9 with the dual moat), so replacing the two separate moat legs with the single value-added-per-worker measure that fuses margin and efficiency should raise the gradient without diluting the -6.8% alpha. Keeping the signal to two legs also stabilizes portfolio composition in the coverage-constrained goodwill subsample.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Capex_Above_Own_Norm_Unproductive
evaluated.expression: SUMRANK(RATIO(RATIO(capx, ppent), MA(RATIO(capx, ppent), 5)), NEG(IND_ADJ(RATIO(sale, emp))))
evaluated.hypothesis: The economically meaningful quantity is how far current investment intensity exceeds the firm's own five-year norm in proportional terms, not merely its ordinal position within that history.
evaluated.reasoning: This isolates an operator-structure choice against the front-runner: a continuous excess-over-own-average ratio instead of TS_RANK, which compresses a firm doubling its normal spending and a firm exceeding it by 5% into the same top rank. If the continuous version improves the slope and the extreme-decile alpha, the mechanism is about the magnitude of the investment shock and the final signal should adopt it; if not, the ordinal state is the right representation and we learn the effect is threshold-like.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Sustained_Research_High_Value_Added_Restraint
evaluated.expression: SUMRANK(IND_ADJ(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), emp)), SUMRANK(RATIO(TS_SUM(xrd, 3), sale), NEG(TS_RANK(RATIO(capx, ppent), 5))))
evaluated.hypothesis: The long side is best defined by a durable research commitment rather than a single year's R&D: firms with three years of cumulative research spending relative to revenue, high value added per worker, and capital spending below their own norm are compounding unrecognized intangible capital.
evaluated.reasoning: The value-added conditioner already lifted the long side to its best result (alpha +3.6%, t=3.56, Sharpe 0.174, FMB 2.36), and the remaining weakness is the noisy single-year R&D leg, which makes membership in the long portfolio unstable; a three-year cumulative research intensity is the natural stock analogue and should raise both the slope and the Sharpe. A credible long leg is necessary because every strong archive result to date is short-side driven.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Equity_Funded_Peak_Expansion_Unproductive
evaluated.expression: SUMRANK(TS_RANK(RATIO(capx, ppent), 5), SUMRANK(RATIO(sstk, at), NEG(IND_ADJ(RATIO(sale, emp)))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Overexpansion is most damaging when it must be funded by selling stock: unproductive firms that issue equity to finance a peak capital-spending cycle combine negative investment and negative financing information, and management is exploiting favorable pricing to fund poor projects.
evaluated.reasoning: Financing has been probed only in isolation — equity issuance as a negative modifier on R&D (gen 1) and debt on intangible collateral (gen 3, wrong sign) — but never as the funding source of the validated peak-capex state, so this tests whether the source of funds adds information beyond the investment state and the intangible deficit. It is the one distinct economic channel in this batch and it keeps near-full coverage since sstk is widely reported.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Triple_Build_Burst_Unproductive
evaluated.expression: SUMRANK(SUMRANK(TS_RANK(RATIO(capx, ppent), 5), SUMRANK(TS_RANK(RATIO(capx, sale), 5), DELTA(RATIO(ppent, ppegt), 1))), NEG(IND_ADJ(RATIO(sale, emp))))
evaluated.hypothesis: A firm is unambiguously overbuilding when capital spending is at a five-year peak against both its installed plant and its revenue base and its asset base is simultaneously getting younger; unproductive operators in this triple-confirmed state destroy value.
evaluated.reasoning: Each of the three investment legs has independently validated evidence (FMB -5.38, -5.61, -4.76) and they measure the same economic event through different accounting windows — cash-flow intensity, demand-relative intensity, and balance-sheet vintage — so requiring agreement should purify the overexpansion state rather than dilute it, as confirmed when the flow-plus-vintage pair beat both of its components on alpha and Sharpe. This is the maximal full-coverage consolidation of everything the search has established.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Build_Burst_Low_Value_Added_Per_Worker
evaluated.expression: SUMRANK(SUMRANK(TS_RANK(RATIO(capx, ppent), 5), DELTA(RATIO(ppent, ppegt), 1)), NEG(IND_ADJ(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), emp))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Value added per worker — gross profit per employee — is the single best summary of a firm's intangible capital, and grading a confirmed build burst by it identifies firms sinking capital into production systems that generate little economic surplus per person.
evaluated.reasoning: This swaps only the conditioner in the archive's best joint signal, testing the one design choice that has repeatedly traded slope for alpha reliability (value added per worker produced t=-5.49 under dual denominators versus -4.98 for revenue per employee). If both metrics hold up, the final signal should use the value-added conditioner because it embeds pricing power and efficiency in one leg instead of two.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Equity_Funded_Build_Burst_Unproductive
evaluated.expression: SUMRANK(SUMRANK(TS_RANK(RATIO(capx, ppent), 5), DELTA(RATIO(ppent, ppegt), 1)), SUMRANK(RATIO(sstk, at), NEG(IND_ADJ(RATIO(sale, emp)))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Overbuilding is worst when it is externally financed: unproductive firms issuing equity while in a confirmed build cycle are funding poor projects with cheap stock, combining adverse investment, financing, and intangible-deficit information.
evaluated.reasoning: The equity-issuance leg delivered the archive's highest Sharpe (-0.562) with only a moderate alpha, indicating it stabilizes the short portfolio's composition month to month rather than deepening the mispricing; attaching it to the strongest build-state signal should therefore raise Sharpe and alpha t together. Coverage stays near 0.11 since stock issuance is broadly reported.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Build_Burst_Goodwill_Overhang
evaluated.expression: SUMRANK(SUMRANK(TS_RANK(RATIO(capx, ppent), 5), DELTA(RATIO(ppent, ppegt), 1)), SUMRANK(RATIO(gdwl, sale), NEG(IND_ADJ(RATIO(sale, emp)))))
evaluated.hypothesis: The deepest short state combines internal overbuilding with a large stock of previously purchased goodwill in a firm that cannot operate efficiently — expansion by both construction and acquisition, unsupported by intangible advantage.
evaluated.reasoning: Goodwill conditioning has produced every alpha beyond -6% in the archive, and pairing it with the dual-denominator capex state already achieved -6.5% with Sharpe -0.552; substituting the better-performing flow-plus-vintage build state should push alpha magnitude further. The cost is coverage near 0.07, which is economically interpretable as restricting attention to acquisitive firms rather than a data artifact.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Sustained_Innovator_Build_Restraint
evaluated.expression: SUMRANK(IND_ADJ(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), emp)), SUMRANK(RATIO(TS_SUM(xrd, 3), sale), NEG(SUMRANK(TS_RANK(RATIO(capx, ppent), 5), DELTA(RATIO(ppent, ppegt), 1)))))
evaluated.hypothesis: The long side is the exact mirror of the short state: high value added per worker, a durable three-year research commitment, and a physical asset base that is neither being expanded nor rejuvenated relative to the firm's own history.
evaluated.reasoning: Replacing single-year R&D with cumulative three-year research improved every long-side metric (alpha +3.8%, t=3.73, Sharpe 0.211, FMB 2.50), so the remaining improvement should come from the restraint leg, which currently uses only the capex flow while the short side has shown that flow and vintage together define the build state far better. Making the long leg the precise complement of the winning short leg should widen the spread and improve the slope.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Build_Burst_With_Unsold_Output
evaluated.expression: SUMRANK(SUMRANK(TS_RANK(RATIO(capx, ppent), 5), SUB(GROWTH(invt, 1), GROWTH(cogs, 1))), NEG(IND_ADJ(RATIO(sale, emp))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Overexpansion becomes visible when new capacity is accompanied by inventory growing faster than the cost of goods sold — capacity already producing goods the market has not absorbed — and this realized demand failure is most damaging for unproductive firms.
evaluated.reasoning: Inventory overhang is the only investment margin in the archive that measures a *realized* rather than planned expansion error (standalone FMB -2.20, alpha -2.4%, t=-2.19), so combining it with the forward-looking capex peak tests whether ex-post demand disappointment adds information to ex-ante capacity building. It runs at near-full coverage and is the one distinct economic channel in this final batch, providing a check that the winning family is not merely a repackaged capital-intensity sort.
evaluated.author: proposer

considered.name: Tangible_Heavy_Asset_Growth
considered.hypothesis: The asset-growth anomaly is concentrated in firms whose balance-sheet expansion is NOT accompanied by knowledge investment; growth that is purely tangible/financial reflects empire building and overinvestment, whereas equally fast growth backed by heavy R&D reflects innovation capital that is mispriced upward.
considered.reasoning: Ranking firms jointly on high asset growth and low R&D intensity isolates "expansion without innovation," which historically earns low subsequent returns, while the R&D leg offsets the penalty for research-intensive growers. Unreported R&D is economically a true zero (non-research firms), so COALESCE is the correct missing-data convention rather than a coverage patch. The interaction is essential: neither asset growth nor R&D intensity alone separates overinvestment from knowledge accumulation.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Bought_vs_Built_Intangibles
considered.hypothesis: Intangible capital acquired through M&A (goodwill creation) reflects premiums paid to targets and integration risk, while intangible capital built internally through R&D is conservatively expensed and undervalued; firms that buy rather than build intangibles underperform.
considered.reasoning: Goodwill additions capitalize the acquirer's overpayment, and prior evidence links acquisitive growth to negative drift and later impairments, whereas organic R&D spending suppresses reported earnings and book equity and is systematically underpriced. Combining the two legs contrasts two routes to the same intangible stock, which is exactly the investment x intangibles interaction. Coverage is protected by treating unreported goodwill and R&D as zero, which is their economic value.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Capacity_Expansion_In_Intangible_Light_Firms
considered.hypothesis: Physical capacity expansion destroys value mainly in industries and firms with no knowledge franchise; in intangible-intensive firms, plant growth is a complement to innovation and carries no negative return implication.
considered.reasoning: The indicator switches the physical-investment signal on only for the below-median R&D-to-sales half of the cross-section, so the portfolio spread is driven by capex-heavy, research-poor firms where competitive erosion and overcapacity are most likely. This is a genuinely conditional interaction: the same gross PP&E growth is given zero weight when the firm is intangible-intensive. Winsorizing the growth leg controls for small-base blowups in the tails.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Identifiable_Intangible_vs_Physical_Formation
considered.hypothesis: Growth in identifiable intangible capital (patents, licenses, technology, customer lists, excluding goodwill) signals a shift of the investment mix toward scalable, high-margin assets, while simultaneous restraint in net physical capital indicates capital discipline; this mix shift predicts higher returns.
considered.reasoning: Stripping goodwill from intangibles removes the acquisition-premium component and leaves the asset class most closely tied to future rents, and netting it against net PP&E growth turns the signal into a pure composition-of-investment measure rather than a scale measure. Markets slowly incorporate mix shifts toward intangible-intensive production because the accounting for identifiable intangibles is heterogeneous and lightly followed. The two legs must be combined; either alone is just a growth-rate variable.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Knowledge_Augmented_Growth_Gap
considered.hypothesis: The gap between reported asset growth and asset growth computed on an R&D-capital-augmented asset base measures how much of a firm's expansion is invisible-to-nobody tangible bloat rather than knowledge accumulation; a positive gap flags firms growing the recorded balance sheet faster than their true (knowledge-inclusive) capital base.
considered.reasoning: Adding a five-year cumulative R&D stock to assets creates the economically correct capital base; the difference between the two growth rates is positive precisely when expansion is tangible-tilted and negative when the firm's true growth engine is expensed research. This is a novel construction because the interaction enters through the denominator/base of the investment measure rather than as a separate ranked leg. Winsorizing limits the influence of small-asset firms with extreme growth rates.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Investment_Mix_Acceleration
considered.hypothesis: What matters is not the level of the investment mix but its second derivative: firms accelerating knowledge investment while decelerating physical capex are reallocating toward intangible production, a transition that depresses current earnings and is therefore underpriced.
considered.reasoning: Acceleration captures fresh managerial reallocation decisions that levels miss, and the two accelerations are jointly required so that the signal does not simply reload on R&D-intensive industries or on the capex anomaly. Firms in this reallocation state report temporarily weak margins and book values, which biases naive valuation screens against them and creates subsequent positive drift. The mechanism is a change-of-change concept, which is why the temporal transformation is justified here rather than cosmetic.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Commodity_Capacity_Expansion
considered.hypothesis: Physical capacity expansion is value-destroying precisely where the firm has no intangible moat; gross margin (industry-adjusted) proxies for brand/technology-based pricing power, so capex growth by low-margin commodity producers signals overinvestment into competitive erosion.
considered.reasoning: The gen-0 conditional capex signal had the right cross-sectional sign but a broken long-short leg partly because a hard indicator threw away half the cross-section and R&D reporting truncated coverage to 12%; replacing the R&D screen with an industry-adjusted gross-margin rank keeps nearly the full universe and grades the intangible franchise continuously. The interaction is essential: high capex growth in high-margin franchises is capacity for rents, while the same growth in low-margin firms is capital destruction.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Self_Financed_Research
considered.hypothesis: Research intensity is rewarded only when it is funded from internal cash flow; R&D funded by fresh equity issuance reflects speculative, cash-burning innovation that the market overprices, whereas internally funded research is conservatively expensed and underpriced.
considered.reasoning: This introduces a financing channel absent from the archive: the same R&D intensity carries opposite information depending on whether the firm must sell stock to pay for it, which links the investment theme (external equity financing) to the intangibles theme (knowledge spending). It should also stabilize the short leg, since issuance-heavy R&D firms are a well-defined, persistently underperforming group rather than an unstable residual.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Bought_vs_Built_Innovation
considered.hypothesis: Firms that acquire their intangible capital through cash acquisitions pay a control premium and face integration risk, while firms that build it internally through R&D understate book value and earnings; buying rather than building innovation predicts low returns.
considered.reasoning: This repairs the rejected gen-0 "bought vs built" idea by using the investment-exclusive acquisition flow (aqc) instead of goodwill, which the validator treats as a shared variable. The two legs contrast two economically substitutable routes to the same intangible stock, so the spread is a pure "make-or-buy" portfolio rather than a restatement of the acquisition anomaly.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Asset_Light_Production_Mix
considered.hypothesis: Holding revenue scale fixed, firms that generate sales from recognized intangible capital rather than from gross physical plant have lower operating leverage, higher scalability, and are systematically underpriced relative to capital-heavy competitors.
considered.reasoning: This tests a stock (production-mix) mechanism rather than the flow/growth mechanisms dominating the archive, and by scaling both asset classes by sales it isolates composition instead of size or growth. Coverage should be high because intan, ppegt, and sale are broadly reported, giving a cleaner read on whether the tangible-versus-intangible distinction pays at the level rather than the change.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Headcount_Growth_Without_Knowledge_Deepening
considered.hypothesis: Labor expansion that dilutes R&D per employee reflects scale-chasing in low-skill capacity, whereas hiring accompanied by rising research spend per worker reflects genuine human-capital deepening; the former predicts low returns.
considered.reasoning: Employment growth is an investment margin that no archive signal has touched, and interacting it with knowledge intensity per worker separates "more bodies" from "better capital per body." The mechanism is a change concept by construction, since the economics concern the direction in which the workforce mix is being reshaped rather than its level.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Knowledge_Share_Reallocation_Trend
considered.hypothesis: A multi-year drift of the investment budget away from physical capex and toward research reflects a durable strategic reallocation toward intangible production; because expensed R&D depresses current earnings while capex is capitalized, this transition mechanically worsens accounting profitability and is underpriced.
considered.reasoning: Gen-0's one-year acceleration version of this idea was directionally right but statistically weak (t=1.31), consistent with single-year investment mix changes being dominated by noise; a five-year trend in the knowledge share extracts the persistent component of the same economic channel. The ratio form also avoids the scale dependence of separately ranked legs and keeps the signal defined for any firm that reports both spending categories.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Overexpansion_Without_Moat
considered.hypothesis: Capacity growth that outruns demand growth is overinvestment, and it is punished most severely in firms with no intangible moat, since low-margin commodity producers cannot earn rents on excess capacity.
considered.reasoning: This refines the best archive signal by netting sales growth out of the capex leg, so the investment channel measures unjustified expansion rather than growth-firm membership, which should sharpen both the FMB slope and the short leg's stability. Coverage stays at the practical maximum because no R&D variable is required, and the moat leg remains industry-adjusted so the sort is not a disguised sector bet.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Make_Or_Buy_Innovation_Share
considered.hypothesis: Over a multi-year window, the fraction of a firm's intangible-capability budget spent buying companies rather than doing research measures its reliance on acquired, premium-priced capabilities; serial buyers underperform serial builders.
considered.reasoning: The gen-1 buy-versus-build signal produced a large FF5 alpha but a zero FMB slope, which indicates a highly skewed, non-monotonic ranked variable driven by a few huge acquisition years; expressing the same economics as a bounded 0-to-1 share over three cumulative years makes the cross-sectional relation approximately monotone while retaining the deal-premium mechanism. Three-year sums also smooth the lumpiness of deal timing, which should raise the Sharpe ratio that was previously essentially zero.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Acquisitive_Expansion_Without_Moat
considered.hypothesis: Acquisitions are most value-destroying when made by firms that lack pricing power of their own, because such buyers are purchasing growth they cannot generate organically and overpay for targets' intangibles.
considered.reasoning: This isolates a specific design question raised by the archive: does the acquisition alpha require the R&D leg (coverage 0.063) or does a high-coverage moat proxy carry the same information at double the sample? Scaling acquisition spend by net physical plant rather than assets makes the leg comparable across capital intensities and emphasizes firms buying capability instead of building it internally.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Goodwill_Overhang_Harvesting
considered.hypothesis: Firms carrying large acquired goodwill relative to the revenue it was supposed to generate, while simultaneously starving their physical asset base of reinvestment, are harvesting past deals and face elevated impairment and decline risk.
considered.reasoning: This is a new channel: it targets the stock of previously purchased intangibles and asks whether the firm is still investing behind it, rather than measuring current investment flows. Goodwill per dollar of sales scales the acquired intangible to its realized output, and the low capex-to-plant leg identifies managers who are no longer supporting the acquired business, a combination that precedes write-downs.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Unrecognized_Knowledge_Capital_Depth
considered.hypothesis: Off-balance-sheet knowledge capital built from five years of expensed research is systematically omitted from book value, so firms whose economic capital is mostly unrecognized research rather than recognized physical plant are undervalued.
considered.reasoning: The failure of the recognized-intangible level mix (Asset_Light_Production_Mix, FMB -0.06) is informative but not decisive, because purchased intangibles on the balance sheet are already priced while expensed R&D stock is precisely the component accounting omits. Running both legs against common book equity makes the comparison a clean statement about which kind of capital dominates the firm's unbooked value, and a null here would let us retire the intangible-level channel entirely and concentrate on expansion flows.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Plant_Expansion_Amid_Productivity_Erosion
considered.hypothesis: Rising gross plant combined with falling revenue per employee signals that the firm is adding hard capacity while its organizational and human-capital efficiency deteriorates, a mix that predicts poor returns.
considered.reasoning: Revenue per employee is a direct proxy for the organizational intangible that converts inputs into sales, and its deterioration alongside physical expansion distinguishes empire building from productive scaling — a channel untouched by the archive's margin- and R&D-based moat proxies. Both legs use widely reported items, so coverage should sit near the sample maximum, and the change-on-change construction is justified because the mechanism is about the direction in which capacity and efficiency are moving apart.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Goodwill_Overhang_Without_Moat
considered.expression: SUMRANK(RATIO(gdwl, sale), SUMRANK(NEG(RATIO(capx, ppent)), NEG(IND_ADJ(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), sale)))))
considered.hypothesis: Firms carrying heavy acquired goodwill per dollar of sales, that are simultaneously starving their physical base of reinvestment and possess no pricing power of their own, are the purest impairment-and-decline candidates in the cross-section.
considered.reasoning: This fuses the archive's largest-alpha channel (goodwill overhang plus harvesting, -6.6%/yr, t=-3.76, but FMB 0.05) with the archive's most monotone channel (industry-adjusted gross margin, FMB -4.5), so the moat leg should supply the linear cross-sectional gradient the goodwill signal lacked while the goodwill leg supplies alpha magnitude. Economically the three legs describe one state: purchased growth, no organic reinvestment, and no rents to defend it.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Stalled_Goodwill_Revenue_Decay
considered.hypothesis: Goodwill impairments are triggered by revenue disappointment at acquired units, so firms whose balance sheet is dominated by acquired intangibles rather than physical plant and whose revenue is now shrinking face imminent write-downs and negative earnings surprises.
considered.reasoning: This isolates the *timing trigger* of the goodwill channel — deteriorating revenue — rather than the reinvestment behavior tested in gen 2, letting us learn which conditioner activates the goodwill overhang. Scaling goodwill by net plant expresses the composition of the asset base as bought-versus-built directly, and revenue decline is the accounting test auditors actually apply.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Debt_Buildup_On_Intangible_Collateral
considered.hypothesis: Intangible-reliant, asset-light firms have little collateral value in liquidation, so debt-financed expansion by such firms raises distress risk and predicts poor returns, whereas the same borrowing by tangible-asset-rich firms is well secured.
considered.reasoning: This is a new financing-mismatch channel: the interaction is between the *form* of new investment financing and the *collateralizability* of the firm's productive assets, which is exactly the tangible-versus-intangible distinction. It uses only widely reported items so coverage should sit at the practical maximum, and it is economically distinct from the equity-issuance version tested in gen 1 (Self_Financed_Research), which spoke to funding cost rather than collateral.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Cash_Buffered_Innovation
considered.hypothesis: R&D is a long-duration, non-collateralizable investment that must be financed from internal liquidity; research-intensive firms that hold large cash buffers can complete projects without dilution or interruption, and this financially unconstrained innovation is underpriced.
considered.reasoning: Gen-1's Self_Financed_Research (R&D intensity minus equity issuance) gave the archive's best positive FMB slope (2.03) but a weak alpha, suggesting the funding-source idea has content but that issuance flow is a noisy conditioner; the cash *stock* is a cleaner, more persistent measure of the capacity to sustain research and should produce steadier portfolio composition. The interaction is essential because cash alone is a weak predictor and R&D alone is an industry bet.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Capex_Growth_Low_Labor_Productivity
considered.hypothesis: Revenue per employee measures the organizational intangible that turns inputs into sales; firms expanding physical investment from a position of structurally low productivity within their industry are adding capacity to an inefficient production system and should underperform.
considered.reasoning: This repairs gen-2's Plant_Expansion_Amid_Productivity_Erosion, whose FMB slope (-2.56) and FF5 alpha (+2.8%) disagreed in sign — a conflict I attribute to the productivity-*growth* leg behaving like a profitability-momentum trend that FF5 leaves in the long leg; using the industry-adjusted productivity *level* keeps the organizational-capital interpretation while removing the trend loading. It also lets us compare two intangible-quality conditioners (gross margin versus labor productivity) applied to the same capex-growth leg.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Knowledge_Share_Of_Investment_Budget
considered.hypothesis: The share of the total investment budget allocated to research rather than physical capital identifies firms whose value creation is expensed rather than capitalized, causing understated earnings and book value and systematic underpricing.
considered.reasoning: The five-year trend in this exact quantity produced a decent FMB slope (2.16) but no alpha, which is consistent with the trend extracting a slow-moving component that portfolio sorts cannot exploit; the level version is a much stronger, more persistent classifier of intangible-versus-tangible business models and should generate a wider, more stable decile spread. Evaluating the level directly against the trend result isolates whether this channel is about the state of the investment mix or its direction of change.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Capex_Growth_Dual_Moat_Deficit
considered.expression: SUMRANK(GROWTH(capx, 1), SUMRANK(NEG(IND_ADJ(RATIO(sale, emp))), NEG(IND_ADJ(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), sale)))))
considered.hypothesis: Physical expansion is most value-destroying when the firm lacks both forms of intangible advantage — pricing power (gross margin) and organizational efficiency (revenue per employee) — because such firms are adding capacity they can neither price nor operate well.
considered.reasoning: The two conditioners produced the archive's two strongest FMB slopes (-5.26 with productivity, -4.51 with margin) but capture different intangibles: rents versus process capital, so combining them should identify a deeper moat deficit than either alone and widen the short leg. Both legs are industry-adjusted and use widely reported items, so coverage stays at the practical maximum and the sort is not a sector bet.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Abnormal_Capacity_Buildup_Unproductive
considered.hypothesis: What matters for overinvestment is not the one-year capex growth rate but whether current capital spending is high relative to the firm's own recent investment history; unproductive firms at a five-year peak of investment intensity are the clearest overexpansion cases.
considered.reasoning: This isolates a single design choice against the front-runner — replacing GROWTH(capx,1) with the firm's position in its own five-year distribution of capex-to-plant — which removes base-year noise and mean-reversion artifacts in growth rates and should improve portfolio stability and Sharpe. If the FMB slope and alpha both strengthen, the channel is about investment *state* rather than the annual change, which would guide the remaining generations.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Total_Hard_Expansion_Unproductive
considered.hypothesis: Capacity purchased through acquisitions and capacity built through capex are economically substitutable ways to expand the hard asset base, and both are penalized when the firm has no organizational productivity advantage to deploy them.
considered.reasoning: The acquisition channel independently generated large alphas but null slopes, while the capex channel generated strong slopes; summing the two flows into one expansion intensity, graded by productivity, tests whether the two investment forms share a single mispricing mechanism and can be measured at full coverage rather than only among R&D reporters. Scaling by net plant keeps the leg comparable across capital intensities.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Goodwill_Overhang_Unproductive_Operator
considered.hypothesis: Acquired goodwill is only justified if the acquirer can run the combined business efficiently; goodwill-laden firms with structurally low revenue per employee have failed to realize synergies and face impairment and margin pressure.
considered.reasoning: This is the targeted repair of the archive's largest-alpha but FMB-null family: substituting the strongest available conditioner (industry-adjusted labor productivity) for the margin/capex conditioners that failed to linearize the goodwill relation in gen 3. Economically it sharpens the story from "harvesting" to "failed integration," which is the observable condition under which goodwill actually gets written down.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Funded_Capital_Light_Innovator
considered.expression: SUMRANK(RATIO(che, at), SUMRANK(RATIO(xrd, sale), NEG(RATIO(capx, sale))))
considered.hypothesis: The mirror image of the overexpansion anomaly is the well-funded, capital-light innovator: a firm that spends on research rather than plant and holds enough liquidity to see projects through, whose value creation is expensed and therefore understated.
considered.reasoning: Three separate long-side channels in the archive each produced positive FF5 alphas of 1.8-3.1% with t between 1.8 and 3.1 but no cross-sectional slope, which suggests each captures a fragment of the same underinvested-in-books firm type; combining liquidity, research intensity, and capex-lightness into one state should raise both alpha reliability and give the FMB slope a monotone gradient. This is the only proposal in the batch aimed at the long side, which matters because all strong archive results are short-side driven.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Inventory_Overhang_Without_Moat
considered.hypothesis: Inventory growing faster than cost of goods sold is unsold capacity — a demand disappointment already funded — and it is most damaging in firms without pricing power, which must discount to clear it, compressing future margins.
considered.reasoning: Working-capital investment is an untested investment margin in this archive, and unlike capex it reveals a realized rather than a planned expansion error, so it should carry information beyond the fixed-capital signals. Netting cogs growth from inventory growth makes the leg a pure overhang measure, and the proven industry-adjusted margin conditioner supplies the intangible interaction at near-maximum coverage.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Peak_Capex_Goodwill_Unproductive
considered.expression: SUMRANK(TS_RANK(RATIO(capx, ppent), 5), SUMRANK(RATIO(gdwl, sale), NEG(IND_ADJ(RATIO(sale, emp)))))
considered.hypothesis: The worst investment state combines both routes to hard-asset expansion — a five-year peak in internal capital spending and a large stock of previously acquired goodwill — in a firm that lacks the organizational productivity to earn a return on either.
considered.reasoning: The two strongest archive signals share the productivity conditioner but differ in the expansion state (peak capex intensity, alpha -5.4%; goodwill overhang, alpha -6.7%), and those states are only weakly overlapping, so fusing them should compound the short-leg alpha rather than dilute it. Unlike gen-4's failed capx-plus-aqc leg, this keeps acquisition exposure as a balance-sheet stock (goodwill) rather than a lumpy annual flow, which is why it should add information instead of noise.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Capex_Per_Revenue_Peak_Unproductive
considered.hypothesis: Capital spending at a five-year high relative to revenue — rather than relative to installed plant — is the sharper statement that capacity is being added ahead of demand, and it is most damaging for firms with low organizational productivity.
considered.reasoning: This isolates one design choice against the front-runner: the scaling denominator of investment intensity, revenue (a demand measure) versus net plant (a capital-stock measure). Because both variables are broadly reported the test runs at full coverage, and the answer tells us whether the mechanism is overcapacity relative to the market or over-replacement of existing assets.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Peak_Capex_Dual_Moat_Deficit
considered.expression: SUMRANK(TS_RANK(RATIO(capx, ppent), 5), SUMRANK(NEG(IND_ADJ(RATIO(sale, emp))), NEG(IND_ADJ(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), sale)))))
considered.hypothesis: Peak-intensity physical expansion is most punished in firms deficient in both intangible advantages — process efficiency and pricing power — since they can neither operate new capacity well nor price its output.
considered.reasoning: With the one-year growth leg, adding the margin conditioner to the productivity conditioner improved alpha from -2.9% to -3.2% and t from -3.35 to -3.51, so the two moat proxies carry partly independent information; pairing them with the much stronger TS_RANK investment state is the natural consolidation at full coverage. If alpha does not improve over Signal 1's family, we learn that productivity alone spans the intangible-quality dimension and can simplify the final signal.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Peak_Capex_Knowledge_Starved
considered.hypothesis: Firms at a multi-year peak of physical investment while spending little on research are substituting bricks for knowledge, and this tangible-tilted allocation of the investment budget predicts low returns.
considered.reasoning: This is the direct tangible-versus-knowledge comparison at the heart of the task, and it repairs gen-0's failed indicator-based version (alpha -0.2%, t=-0.21) by replacing the discarded-half conditional and the noisy one-year growth leg with the proven continuous R&D-intensity rank and the five-year investment state. Comparing it to the productivity-conditioned version tells us whether the intangible ingredient that matters is realized organizational output or reported research spending, with coverage restricted to R&D reporters as the known cost.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Productive_Research_Capex_Restraint
considered.expression: SUMRANK(IND_ADJ(RATIO(sale, emp)), SUMRANK(RATIO(xrd, sale), NEG(TS_RANK(RATIO(capx, ppent), 5))))
considered.hypothesis: The mirror of the overexpansion anomaly is a highly productive, research-intensive firm that is deliberately restraining physical capital spending relative to its own history; its value creation is expensed and its capital discipline is unrewarded in accounting profitability.
considered.reasoning: Every reliable archive result is short-side driven, and the long-side channels (cash-buffered innovation, funded capital-light innovator) delivered ~3% alphas with t>3 but zero FMB slope, indicating a poorly graded cross-section; importing the two ingredients that created gradient on the short side — industry-adjusted productivity and the five-year investment state — should give the long side a monotone slope as well. This is a substantive reconstruction rather than a variant, because it replaces the liquidity leg with a productivity leg on the theory that unrecognized intangible capital shows up as output per worker.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Identifiable_Intangible_Formation_vs_Plant
considered.hypothesis: Investment directed into identifiable intangibles — patents, technology, licenses, customer relationships, excluding goodwill — reflects capability building with durable rents, whereas peak-intensity plant spending reflects commodity capacity; firms tilting toward plant and away from intangible formation underperform.
considered.reasoning: The archive has tested recognized intangible *levels* (which failed, FMB -0.06) but never recognized intangible *formation flows*, which are the true investment-side analogue of capex and are available for far more firms than R&D. Netting goodwill out of the change in intangibles removes acquisition premiums, so the leg measures purchased capability rather than deal accounting, making this a genuinely new comparison within the investment budget.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Dual_Denominator_Peak_Capex_Unproductive
considered.expression: SUMRANK(SUMRANK(TS_RANK(RATIO(capx, ppent), 5), TS_RANK(RATIO(capx, sale), 5)), NEG(IND_ADJ(RATIO(sale, emp))))
considered.hypothesis: A firm is unambiguously overexpanding when capital spending is simultaneously at a five-year peak relative to its installed plant and relative to its revenue base; conditioned on low organizational productivity, this doubly-confirmed capacity buildup should be the strongest short state in the cross-section.
considered.reasoning: The two normalizations produced the archive's best alpha and best FMB slope respectively, and they can disagree — a firm replacing old plant without adding capacity scores high on one and low on the other — so requiring both should purify the overinvestment state and improve both metrics at once. Coverage stays near maximum since only capx, ppent, sale, and emp are needed.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Peak_Capex_Persistent_Low_Productivity
considered.hypothesis: Organizational capital is a slow-moving stock, so a three-year average of industry-adjusted revenue per employee measures it better than a single noisy year, and grading peak capital spending by this persistent measure should improve both the slope and the stability of the short leg.
considered.reasoning: This isolates one design choice — smoothing the intangible conditioner — against the best-FMB signal in the archive, holding the investment leg fixed. If alpha and Sharpe improve, the mispricing is about structural organizational weakness rather than a transitory productivity dip, which would guide the final consolidation; if it degrades, the conditioner is picking up recent operating news and should stay unsmoothed.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Fresh_Plant_Unproductive_Operator
considered.hypothesis: The undepreciated share of gross plant measures how recently a firm's physical capacity was built; a young, largely unamortized asset base in the hands of a firm with weak organizational productivity represents freshly sunk capital that will not earn its cost.
considered.reasoning: This is a new state variable — capital vintage from the ppent-to-ppegt ratio — that summarizes years of cumulative physical expansion in a single persistent stock measure, rather than the flow-based peaks tested so far, so it should generate low-turnover portfolios and test whether the anomaly is about the spending act or the resulting capital overhang. It requires only widely reported items, so coverage should match the front-runners.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Goodwill_Overhang_Dual_Moat
considered.expression: SUMRANK(RATIO(gdwl, sale), SUMRANK(NEG(IND_ADJ(RATIO(sale, emp))), NEG(IND_ADJ(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), sale)))))
considered.hypothesis: Acquired goodwill is most likely to be impaired when the acquirer can neither operate efficiently nor price with power, so grading goodwill intensity by both intangible-advantage deficits should identify failed integrations with a monotone gradient rather than only in the tail.
considered.reasoning: The goodwill family carries the archive's largest alphas (-6.6% to -6.7%, |t|>4) but its FMB slope has never exceeded -2.4, and productivity conditioning was the only thing that moved it; adding the second, partly independent moat proxy is the natural next step to linearize the relation without diluting the alpha. Coverage will remain near 0.078 because goodwill reporting is the binding constraint, which is an accepted cost for this specific channel.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Funded_Productive_Innovator_Capex_Discipline
considered.expression: SUMRANK(IND_ADJ(RATIO(sale, emp)), SUMRANK(SUMRANK(RATIO(xrd, sale), RATIO(che, at)), NEG(TS_RANK(RATIO(capx, ppent), 5))))
considered.hypothesis: The long-side counterpart of the anomaly is a productive, research-intensive, cash-funded firm that is holding physical capital spending below its own historical norm; its economic capital is expensed and its restraint is misread as lack of growth.
considered.reasoning: Two independent long-side channels each delivered roughly 3% alpha with t near 3.1 — liquidity-plus-research and productivity-plus-research-plus-restraint — and only the latter produced a positive FMB slope (2.43), so combining the liquidity leg with the productivity-graded version should raise alpha reliability while preserving the gradient. This is the only long-side proposal in the batch, which matters because a tradable spread needs a defensible long leg, not just a short leg.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Erratic_Capital_Budget_Weak_Organization
considered.hypothesis: Volatile capital spending relative to revenue indicates an undisciplined, stop-start investment policy; in firms that also lack organizational productivity it signals weak governance and poor project selection, predicting low returns.
considered.reasoning: This opens a second-moment channel never tested in the archive — the instability rather than the level or peak of investment intensity — and it is economically distinct because a firm can have volatile investment without ever reaching a five-year peak. Pairing it with the proven productivity conditioner keeps the intangible interaction intact at full coverage, and a null result would usefully confirm that only the level/state of overexpansion is priced.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Peak_Capex_Goodwill_Dual_Moat
considered.expression: SUMRANK(SUMRANK(TS_RANK(RATIO(capx, ppent), 5), TS_RANK(RATIO(capx, sale), 5)), SUMRANK(RATIO(gdwl, sale), NEG(IND_ADJ(RATIO(sale, emp)))))
considered.hypothesis: The maximal short state combines doubly-confirmed peak internal capacity spending with a large stock of acquired goodwill in a firm that lacks the organizational productivity to earn a return on either form of expansion.
considered.reasoning: The goodwill state contributes the archive's largest alphas (-6.6% to -6.8%) and the dual-denominator capex state contributes the strongest slope (-5.72), and gen 5 showed their two-leg fusion raised Sharpe to -0.545, so upgrading the capex side to both denominators should push alpha and Sharpe further while partially preserving the gradient. The accepted cost is coverage near 0.07, driven by goodwill reporting, which is a genuine economic restriction to acquisitive firms rather than a data artifact.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Dual_Peak_Capex_Dual_Moat_Deficit
considered.expression: SUMRANK(SUMRANK(TS_RANK(RATIO(capx, ppent), 5), TS_RANK(RATIO(capx, sale), 5)), SUMRANK(NEG(IND_ADJ(RATIO(sale, emp))), NEG(IND_ADJ(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), sale)))))
considered.hypothesis: Peak-intensity physical expansion confirmed on both scaling bases, in firms deficient in both pricing power and operating efficiency, identifies overinvestment without intangible support at full sample coverage.
considered.reasoning: This is the symmetric, full-coverage consolidation of the two proven design axes — two investment legs and two intangible legs — and gen 5 showed the margin conditioner adds alpha on top of productivity (from -5.4% to -4.7% with one denominator, with t improving in the dual-moat case). Because it needs no goodwill or R&D data it should retain coverage near 0.117 and thus be the more robust candidate if its metrics approach Signal 1's.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Dual_Peak_Capex_Low_Value_Added_Per_Worker
considered.expression: SUMRANK(SUMRANK(TS_RANK(RATIO(capx, ppent), 5), TS_RANK(RATIO(capx, sale), 5)), NEG(IND_ADJ(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), emp))))
considered.hypothesis: Gross profit per employee is the sharpest single measure of a firm's intangible capital, since it combines pricing power and labor efficiency into value added per worker; peak physical expansion by firms with low value added per worker is the cleanest overinvestment state.
considered.reasoning: The two conditioners that worked separately — margin and revenue per employee — are both partial views of value added per worker, so measuring it directly should dominate them in a single parsimonious leg rather than requiring two ranked legs that dilute each other. This is a substantive conditioner upgrade, not a restatement, and it keeps full coverage while reducing the signal to one investment concept and one intangible concept.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: High_Value_Added_Innovator_Capex_Restraint
considered.expression: SUMRANK(IND_ADJ(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), emp)), SUMRANK(RATIO(xrd, sale), NEG(TS_RANK(RATIO(capx, ppent), 5))))
considered.hypothesis: Firms generating high value added per worker, spending heavily on research, and holding physical capital spending below their own historical norm are compounding unrecognized intangible capital and are underpriced.
considered.reasoning: The long side has stabilized at roughly +3% alpha with t near 3.1 and a positive slope of about 2.4, and its weakest element is the conditioner, so substituting value added per worker for raw revenue per employee should raise the gradient by separating high-price, high-efficiency firms from low-margin revenue churners. A stronger long leg matters for the final signal because every reliable result so far is short-side driven.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Capital_Deepening_Peak_Without_Pricing_Power
considered.hypothesis: A five-year peak in physical capital per employee means the firm has substituted machines for people; without pricing power to monetize the new capital intensity, this deepening locks in fixed costs and depresses future returns.
considered.reasoning: This introduces a new investment state — the capital-labor mix rather than the flow of spending — which can be at a peak even when capex intensity is not, for instance after headcount cuts, so it tests a distinguishable form of tangible-heavy commitment. Pairing it with the margin conditioner rather than productivity avoids mechanical overlap between the employment term in both legs, and both inputs are broadly reported.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Plant_Rejuvenation_Burst_Unproductive
considered.hypothesis: A rising undepreciated share of gross plant means the firm has just installed a burst of new capacity relative to its existing stock; when the operator is unproductive, this newly sunk capital signals a value-destroying build cycle.
considered.reasoning: This repairs gen-6's Fresh_Plant_Unproductive_Operator, whose slope was the archive's strongest (-6.04) but whose alpha was negligible (t=-1.55) because a static vintage level is highly persistent and largely spanned by the FF5 investment and profitability factors; taking the annual change isolates the fresh building event, which should be far less factor-spanned and therefore carry portfolio alpha. It also tests the level-versus-change question on a stock-based capacity measure, complementing the flow-based peak results.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Peak_Capex_Low_Value_Added_Per_Worker
considered.hypothesis: Physical capital spending at a five-year peak relative to installed plant, undertaken by firms whose value added per worker is low for their industry, is the cleanest statement of tangible overexpansion without intangible capital to support it.
considered.reasoning: This fills the one untested cell of the archive's design grid: the single best-alpha investment leg paired with the best-alpha conditioner, both of which have been validated separately (alpha -5.4% with productivity; alpha t=-5.49 with value added per worker under two denominators). Parsimony matters here because each additional ranked leg has cost slope strength, so a two-leg version should retain the -5.4 FMB while capturing the value-added conditioner's alpha reliability at full coverage.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Flow_And_Vintage_Build_Burst_Unproductive
considered.expression: SUMRANK(SUMRANK(TS_RANK(RATIO(capx, ppent), 5), DELTA(RATIO(ppent, ppegt), 1)), NEG(IND_ADJ(RATIO(sale, emp))))
considered.hypothesis: A firm is unambiguously in a build cycle when its spending flow is at a multi-year peak and its plant is simultaneously getting younger relative to gross cost; unproductive operators in this state have just sunk capital they cannot monetize.
considered.reasoning: The vintage-change leg is an independently validated build measure (FMB -4.76, alpha -3.5%, t=-3.42) built from balance-sheet stocks rather than the cash-flow statement, so it carries information the capex flow misses — for instance disposals of old plant alongside new construction. Fusing a flow measure with a stock measure of the same economic event should sharpen the short leg more than stacking two flow normalizations did in gen 6.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Goodwill_Overhang_Low_Value_Added
considered.hypothesis: Acquired goodwill is impaired when the combined firm cannot generate value added per employee; goodwill-heavy firms with low gross profit per worker have demonstrably failed to realize the synergies they paid for.
considered.reasoning: The goodwill family holds the archive's largest alphas, and its slope responded only to productivity conditioning (from 0.05 to -2.4, then -2.9 with the dual moat), so replacing the two separate moat legs with the single value-added-per-worker measure that fuses margin and efficiency should raise the gradient without diluting the -6.8% alpha. Keeping the signal to two legs also stabilizes portfolio composition in the coverage-constrained goodwill subsample.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Capex_Above_Own_Norm_Unproductive
considered.expression: SUMRANK(RATIO(RATIO(capx, ppent), MA(RATIO(capx, ppent), 5)), NEG(IND_ADJ(RATIO(sale, emp))))
considered.hypothesis: The economically meaningful quantity is how far current investment intensity exceeds the firm's own five-year norm in proportional terms, not merely its ordinal position within that history.
considered.reasoning: This isolates an operator-structure choice against the front-runner: a continuous excess-over-own-average ratio instead of TS_RANK, which compresses a firm doubling its normal spending and a firm exceeding it by 5% into the same top rank. If the continuous version improves the slope and the extreme-decile alpha, the mechanism is about the magnitude of the investment shock and the final signal should adopt it; if not, the ordinal state is the right representation and we learn the effect is threshold-like.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Sustained_Research_High_Value_Added_Restraint
considered.expression: SUMRANK(IND_ADJ(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), emp)), SUMRANK(RATIO(TS_SUM(xrd, 3), sale), NEG(TS_RANK(RATIO(capx, ppent), 5))))
considered.hypothesis: The long side is best defined by a durable research commitment rather than a single year's R&D: firms with three years of cumulative research spending relative to revenue, high value added per worker, and capital spending below their own norm are compounding unrecognized intangible capital.
considered.reasoning: The value-added conditioner already lifted the long side to its best result (alpha +3.6%, t=3.56, Sharpe 0.174, FMB 2.36), and the remaining weakness is the noisy single-year R&D leg, which makes membership in the long portfolio unstable; a three-year cumulative research intensity is the natural stock analogue and should raise both the slope and the Sharpe. A credible long leg is necessary because every strong archive result to date is short-side driven.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Equity_Funded_Peak_Expansion_Unproductive
considered.expression: SUMRANK(TS_RANK(RATIO(capx, ppent), 5), SUMRANK(RATIO(sstk, at), NEG(IND_ADJ(RATIO(sale, emp)))))
considered.hypothesis: Overexpansion is most damaging when it must be funded by selling stock: unproductive firms that issue equity to finance a peak capital-spending cycle combine negative investment and negative financing information, and management is exploiting favorable pricing to fund poor projects.
considered.reasoning: Financing has been probed only in isolation — equity issuance as a negative modifier on R&D (gen 1) and debt on intangible collateral (gen 3, wrong sign) — but never as the funding source of the validated peak-capex state, so this tests whether the source of funds adds information beyond the investment state and the intangible deficit. It is the one distinct economic channel in this batch and it keeps near-full coverage since sstk is widely reported.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Triple_Build_Burst_Unproductive
considered.expression: SUMRANK(SUMRANK(TS_RANK(RATIO(capx, ppent), 5), SUMRANK(TS_RANK(RATIO(capx, sale), 5), DELTA(RATIO(ppent, ppegt), 1))), NEG(IND_ADJ(RATIO(sale, emp))))
considered.hypothesis: A firm is unambiguously overbuilding when capital spending is at a five-year peak against both its installed plant and its revenue base and its asset base is simultaneously getting younger; unproductive operators in this triple-confirmed state destroy value.
considered.reasoning: Each of the three investment legs has independently validated evidence (FMB -5.38, -5.61, -4.76) and they measure the same economic event through different accounting windows — cash-flow intensity, demand-relative intensity, and balance-sheet vintage — so requiring agreement should purify the overexpansion state rather than dilute it, as confirmed when the flow-plus-vintage pair beat both of its components on alpha and Sharpe. This is the maximal full-coverage consolidation of everything the search has established.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Build_Burst_Low_Value_Added_Per_Worker
considered.expression: SUMRANK(SUMRANK(TS_RANK(RATIO(capx, ppent), 5), DELTA(RATIO(ppent, ppegt), 1)), NEG(IND_ADJ(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), emp))))
considered.hypothesis: Value added per worker — gross profit per employee — is the single best summary of a firm's intangible capital, and grading a confirmed build burst by it identifies firms sinking capital into production systems that generate little economic surplus per person.
considered.reasoning: This swaps only the conditioner in the archive's best joint signal, testing the one design choice that has repeatedly traded slope for alpha reliability (value added per worker produced t=-5.49 under dual denominators versus -4.98 for revenue per employee). If both metrics hold up, the final signal should use the value-added conditioner because it embeds pricing power and efficiency in one leg instead of two.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Equity_Funded_Build_Burst_Unproductive
considered.expression: SUMRANK(SUMRANK(TS_RANK(RATIO(capx, ppent), 5), DELTA(RATIO(ppent, ppegt), 1)), SUMRANK(RATIO(sstk, at), NEG(IND_ADJ(RATIO(sale, emp)))))
considered.hypothesis: Overbuilding is worst when it is externally financed: unproductive firms issuing equity while in a confirmed build cycle are funding poor projects with cheap stock, combining adverse investment, financing, and intangible-deficit information.
considered.reasoning: The equity-issuance leg delivered the archive's highest Sharpe (-0.562) with only a moderate alpha, indicating it stabilizes the short portfolio's composition month to month rather than deepening the mispricing; attaching it to the strongest build-state signal should therefore raise Sharpe and alpha t together. Coverage stays near 0.11 since stock issuance is broadly reported.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Build_Burst_Goodwill_Overhang
considered.expression: SUMRANK(SUMRANK(TS_RANK(RATIO(capx, ppent), 5), DELTA(RATIO(ppent, ppegt), 1)), SUMRANK(RATIO(gdwl, sale), NEG(IND_ADJ(RATIO(sale, emp)))))
considered.hypothesis: The deepest short state combines internal overbuilding with a large stock of previously purchased goodwill in a firm that cannot operate efficiently — expansion by both construction and acquisition, unsupported by intangible advantage.
considered.reasoning: Goodwill conditioning has produced every alpha beyond -6% in the archive, and pairing it with the dual-denominator capex state already achieved -6.5% with Sharpe -0.552; substituting the better-performing flow-plus-vintage build state should push alpha magnitude further. The cost is coverage near 0.07, which is economically interpretable as restricting attention to acquisitive firms rather than a data artifact.

considered.name: Sustained_Innovator_Build_Restraint
considered.expression: SUMRANK(IND_ADJ(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), emp)), SUMRANK(RATIO(TS_SUM(xrd, 3), sale), NEG(SUMRANK(TS_RANK(RATIO(capx, ppent), 5), DELTA(RATIO(ppent, ppegt), 1)))))
considered.hypothesis: The long side is the exact mirror of the short state: high value added per worker, a durable three-year research commitment, and a physical asset base that is neither being expanded nor rejuvenated relative to the firm's own history.
considered.reasoning: Replacing single-year R&D with cumulative three-year research improved every long-side metric (alpha +3.8%, t=3.73, Sharpe 0.211, FMB 2.50), so the remaining improvement should come from the restraint leg, which currently uses only the capex flow while the short side has shown that flow and vintage together define the build state far better. Making the long leg the precise complement of the winning short leg should widen the spread and improve the slope.

considered.name: Build_Burst_With_Unsold_Output
considered.expression: SUMRANK(SUMRANK(TS_RANK(RATIO(capx, ppent), 5), SUB(GROWTH(invt, 1), GROWTH(cogs, 1))), NEG(IND_ADJ(RATIO(sale, emp))))
considered.hypothesis: Overexpansion becomes visible when new capacity is accompanied by inventory growing faster than the cost of goods sold — capacity already producing goods the market has not absorbed — and this realized demand failure is most damaging for unproductive firms.
considered.reasoning: Inventory overhang is the only investment margin in the archive that measures a *realized* rather than planned expansion error (standalone FMB -2.20, alpha -2.4%, t=-2.19), so combining it with the forward-looking capex peak tests whether ex-post demand disappointment adds information to ex-ante capacity building. It runs at near-full coverage and is the one distinct economic channel in this final batch, providing a check that the winning family is not merely a repackaged capital-intensity sort.
